01
Position package

Age assurance without ID-checking every adult

Answers producing a position package end-to-end. A full package on one live, contested issue: bottom line, hostile FAQ, talking points for three audiences, fact sheet, and the log of disagreements I would close before it ships.

Bottom line

Support a federal floor that requires age assurance in proportion to risk, puts the heaviest duties on features that simulate relationships, and protects adults' privacy: age estimation first, identity checks only on escalation.

Why now. Washington now requires AI disclosure and break reminders every three hours in long conversations; Idaho, Nebraska and Oregon have enacted companion-chatbot laws. The GUARD Act cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee unanimously. China's rules for human-like AI companions took effect on 15 July 2026. The administration has asked Congress not to preempt state child-safety laws, so a patchwork is the default.

The gap in current drafts. Definitions turn on systems "designed to encourage" emotional interaction. Without clear tests, general assistants that are simply warm in tone could be swept in, and age verification done through ID checks would build large stores of adults' identity data.

Pillar 1Regulate by function, not label

Persistent personas, relationship simulation and design for emotional reliance trigger the strongest duties.

Pillar 2Privacy-preserving assurance first

Self-declaration, then estimation, then verification only on escalation; verification data deleted after the check.

Pillar 3A duty of care where minors may be present

Disclosure, no sexual content, no romantic roleplay with minors, crisis-intervention routes.

Pillar 4A federal floor, not a ceiling

Consistent with preempting states only where federal law is at least as strong.

We would support
  • AI disclosure and break reminders
  • Crisis duties; bans on sexual content involving minors
  • Independent accuracy testing of age estimation across groups
We would push to change
  • Government-ID checks for every adult
  • Companion definitions that capture all assistants
  • Liability for good-faith estimation errors without an audited safe harbour

Your consumer product already requires users to be 18. Why legislate?

Terms of service verify nothing, and many products built on frontier models sit with third parties. A floor protects children across the ecosystem and stops responsible developers being undercut.

Isn't "proportionate" a loophole?

It is tied to named features, not a company's own judgement, and regulators can audit the written risk assessment.

Age estimation errs more for some groups. Acceptable?

Only with published accuracy testing across groups, an appeal route, and escalation instead of lockout.

Why not back the GUARD Act as written?

We share its aims. Two asks: clear functional tests in the companion definition, and let privacy-preserving methods meet the age-verification duty instead of ID checks for every user.

Doesn't a federal standard wipe out state protections?

Not under this position. It is a floor; states can go further.

How does this square with your own identity checks?

Fair, and logged as contested point 4. The answer must be public and consistent before deployment.

Federal · Hill staff
  • Children already use AI companions. One national floor beats 50 rulebooks with gaps.
  • We share the GUARD Act's core aim: no sexual content with minors and no chatbot that encourages self-harm.
  • Target relationship simulation, not every helpful assistant.
  • Protect adults too: estimation first, ID only on escalation.
State · legislators
  • Disclosure and break reminders, as in Washington, are cheap and work.
  • Write duties by function so statutes stay current.
  • Align definitions with neighbouring states.
  • A strong federal floor leaves your authority to go further intact.
International · regulators
  • Companion AI is now its own category: China's measures took effect in July 2026.
  • Shared vocabulary: the best interests of the child, per UN CRC General Comment No. 25.
  • Make age-assurance standards interoperable across regulators.
  • Bring privacy authorities in from the start.

02
Translation

One framework, three readers

Answers policy-ready language for federal, state, and international policymakers. The same frontier-AI proposal, rewritten for a Hill staffer, a state legislator and an international regulator, with what I cut for each.

Source: the Advanced AI Framework, 10 June 2026. Mandatory pre-deployment testing for models trained above 1025 FLOPs, where the developer also has over $500M in AI revenue or over $1B in AI R&D. Four test areas: biological-weapons uplift, large-scale cyber-vulnerability discovery, loss of control of autonomous systems, automated AI R&D. Governments could block models that fail. A proposal, not law.

Certify the most powerful models the way we certify aircraft

  • Who is covered: only the largest developers, by compute and revenue tests. Press reports name about five.
  • What it asks: independent tests in four high-consequence areas, plus weight security and incident reporting.
  • The vote your boss faces: whether a federal body may block a model that fails.
  • The question you will get: does it override state law? Only where the federal standard is at least as strong.

// cut: the Economic Policy Framework, which goes to other committees

Your laws stay; frontier testing moves to Washington

  • What survives: California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois's SB 315 remain the floor.
  • Where you still lead: deployment, consumer protection, children, public-sector use.
  • What to avoid: state-level frontier testing, which needs national technical capacity.
  • What to ask for: federal test results shared with state regulators.

// cut: penalty design and revenue thresholds, which are federal matters

The threshold you already use, with a stronger stop button

  • Familiar ground: 1025 FLOPs is where the EU AI Act presumes systemic risk for general-purpose models.
  • Overlap: the four test areas line up with EU systemic-risk evaluation.
  • The difference: explicit authority to block deployment, with revenue-linked penalties.
  • The opening: mutual recognition of results from government-authorised testers.

// cut: US preemption politics, which do not travel

03
Message testing

Which case for testing lands, and with whom

Answers bringing rigor to what lands and why. Four framings of one position and the test design to compare them across four audience segments. No results until real responses exist.

AWAITING FIELDWORKThis is the design. Meters stay empty until real responses exist; nothing here is a finding.
Frame A · Safety
We test aircraft before they carry passengers. The most powerful AI systems should pass independent safety tests before release too.
signal

Hypothesis: strong everywhere, weakest on credibility with technical readers.

Frame B · Competitiveness
Countries lead when their technology is trusted. Independent testing is how frontier developers prove their systems are safe enough to adopt.
signal

Hypothesis: strongest with US economic audiences, weakest abroad.

Frame C · Consumer protection
Companies should not grade their own homework. Independent testers should check the most powerful models before they reach families and businesses.
signal

Hypothesis: leads with generalist policy staff in every region.

Frame D · National security
The most capable AI can find software vulnerabilities at scale. Testing before release keeps those capabilities out of the wrong hands.
signal

Hypothesis: leads with US security audiences, trails internationally.

Method
  • 30 to 40 policy professionals in four segments: US, EU and UK, Asia-Pacific, Global South.
  • All four frames, randomised order, rated 1 to 7 on persuasiveness and credibility.
  • Most and least convincing, plus the first objection that comes to mind.
Read-out and limits
  • Mean scores by segment, net best-minus-worst, objections coded into themes.
  • A convenience sample: direction, not proof.
  • At scale: a professional panel, matched controls, a second round on the winner.
